pr_title: ESQL: Ask for correct field names if only LOOKUP/ENRICH fields are kept
pr_body:
Fixes https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/120272

# Some context on the bug

The issue occurs as follows, top-down (Read linked issue for context on the bug):
- A query like `FROM index | EVAL x = 1 | LOOKUP l ON x | KEEP lookup_field` returns no rows. Exactly the same with ENRICH
- It returns no rows because the FROM relationship is replaced by an EMPTY LocalRelationship
- The EMPTY rel comes from the EsIndex having no concrete indices
- It has no concrete indices because field-caps returns no results for that index+fields
- The fields come from fieldNames(), which must return an existing field, or _index if there's no field to query
- There's a logic in fieldNames() that says "If no fields, then use _index". It's not working, because the fields requested from LOOKUP appear in the list of fields

# Potential solution

Givens:
- We don't know which fields every lookup returns, so we can't substract them from the list
- We would have to first make the field-caps for lookup
- But the field-caps requets for lookup depends on the results of fieldNames()

Which means we will probably have to reorganize the `EsqlSession.analyzedPlan()` code to correctly trace every field.

# Current solution

This PR's solution is a simple, lazy one. It works well apparently, and I suppose it wasn't done before to try to keep the fieldNames "exact". But since enrich&lookup, it wasn't exact anymore, and we were asking for enrich/lookup index fields indistinctly.

Consider this a temporary solution until analyzedPlan() and fieldNames() get a refactor

issue_context.title: ESQL: No rows with JOIN/ENRICH + EVAL + KEEP
issue_context.body:
Weird interaction resulting in no rows:

Correct:
```
FROM languages
| DROP language_code
| EVAL language_code = 3
| LOOKUP JOIN languages_lookup ON language_code

# Results:
 language_code | language_name 
---------------+---------------
3              |Spanish
3              |Spanish
3              |Spanish
3              |Spanish
```

Wrong results:
```
FROM languages
| DROP language_code
| EVAL language_code = 3
| LOOKUP JOIN languages_lookup ON language_code
| KEEP language_code

# Results:
 language_code 
---------------
```

You can remove the first DROP if the original index doesn't have the JOIN key column
comments:
After some investigation, it's happening because of `fieldNames()` returning fields from the lookup to be searched through field-caps, which return no concrete indices for them.

The same is also happening with `ENRICH`, also in 8.17.

Also, chaining any of those commands may render a similar result: They will add "their own fields" to the field_caps

The actual problem seems to be, as @ivancea pointed out offline, the premature elimination of an `EsRelation` from the logical nodes tree which is removed with `PruneEmptyPlans` thus making the query a `LocalRelation` one - in other words, not reaching ES at all.

There is a set of three major use cases here, that are covered by the same set of code:
- `from employees | keep height | drop height | eval x = 1 | stats c=count(x), mi=min(x), s=sum(x)` this eliminates all the columns from `employees` thus indicating there is no need for `employees` to be queried, but the follow up `eval` creates a new column and runs some `stats` on it. This **correctly** returns 0 and `null`.
- `from employees | drop languages | eval languages = 123 | keep languages` this tells the `field_caps` call we make to only look at  the field `languages`, gets the information for it, creates an `EsRelation[languages]` then drops the `languages` from the logical plan, creates another column with the same name and keeps only that. This use case is not covered **now** in our code, like we cover the `stats` use case above. This logical plan ends up **incorrectly** as a `LocalRelation`.
- the same as the previous use case: `from employees | drop height | eval x = 1 | stats c=count(*), count(x)`. This one shouldn't return 0, but it does. It should return as the number of rows in `employees`.

The last two use cases have something in common: they just need a count of documents from ES, they don't need the actual rows.
This has been identified as such some time ago in [this issue](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/98703). The first use case is in the same ballpark: it doesn't need the rows of `employees`, and it's setting the number of rows to 0 because all the columns (**and implicitly all the rows**) have been eliminated.

```
from employees | drop languages | eval languages = 123 | keep languages
```
I think the problem is that due to the field caps call, we act as if `languages` was the only field that `employees` has, and then dropping the field leads to an empty relation. But that's wrong in general, there normally are other fields - at the very least metadata fields when we use `from employees metadata _index`, for example. But when `languages` is the only actual field, this can be considered right again!

Particularly nasty is when an index' mapping changes. Let's consider an index pattern instead:
```
from emp* | drop languages | eval languages = 123 | keep languages
```
Maybe at first, there's only `employees` and this has only the `languages` field and thus an empty result is correct. Then we add another index `employees2` with an additional field `languages_2` - and suddenly, you get `123` as many times as there are rows in both `employees` and `employees2`. The rows of `employees` suddenly start to contribute.

The same happens when we ask for metadata fields in the `from`: 
```
from employees metadata _index | drop languages | eval languages = 123 | keep languages
```
Because `employees` only has the `languages` field (in my examples), omitting the `metadata` will correctly result in an empty result, while adding it to the `from` clause makes this return `123` as many times as there are docs in `employees`. Even though `_index` doesn't make it into the output of the query, at all.

This makes me think that it's actually bad that we consider a result with 0 columns and 10 rows equivalent to one with no rows whatsoever. Such a plan would be equivalent to a `DROP *`, anyway, which we consider invalid.

Coming back to your first example @astefan:
```
from employees | keep height | drop height | eval x = 1 | stats c=count(x), mi=min(x), s=sum(x)
```
If this returned the total count number of documents for `c`, instead, I think overall we'd have more consistency. And less edge cases to consider.

**TL'DR: Maybe we shouldn't prune empty relations and, in the case that we don't need any fields from an index, still determine how many documents it has. Or, for simplicity, just consider a query invalid if it does not use any fields and also doesn't compute `count(*)`.**

In practical terms, the former means `PruneEmptyPlans` and `PropagateEmptyRelations` would need to be removed, and we'd have to deal with whatever hickups with the compute engine this will mean.

The latter would be easier to implement - we'd just have to walk down the plan and check if at any point the plan does not have any dependencies on field attributes. Similar logic already exists in `ProjectAwayColumns`.

Further research and analysis results on this issue and some very subtle behaviors of ES|QL.

1. `from employees | keep height | drop height | eval x = 1 | stats c=count(x)`

This is a query where we could easily tell that if we keep one field and then we drop it, this means that ES|QL **doesn't need any fields from ES** and turns  this query in a 0-columns result which also **drops all its data. No columns == no data was introduced some time ago.** Of course, this is a very specific use case. There are other variants of it: `keep height* | drop height*`, `keep onefield, twofields | drop onefield | drop two*` etc. I guess it's mostly about keeping something and dropping more or less the same thing.

Atm, this query **works ok** by recognizing an empty output projections list:

```
Rule analysis.Analyzer$ResolveRefs applied
Aggregate[STANDARD,[],[COUNT(?x,true[BOOLEAN]) AS c]]                                ! Aggregate[STANDARD,[],[COUNT(x{r}#4,true[BOOLEAN]) AS c]]
\_Eval[[1[INTEGER] AS x]]                                                            = \_Eval[[1[INTEGER] AS x]]
  \_Drop[[?height]]                        ---------------->                         !   \_EsqlProject[[]] 
    \_Keep[[?height]]                                                                !     \_EsqlProject[[height{f}#9]]
      \_EsRelation[employees][height{f}#9, height.float{f}#12, height.half_float{..] =       \_EsRelation[employees][height{f}#9, height.float{f}#12, height.half_float{..]
```

2. `from employees | drop salary | eval salary = 1 | keep salary`

A very similar query to the one above, which **doesn't work atm** (!!!) and in the same ballpark idea as the one I [mentioned previously](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/120272#issuecomment-2607081076) has the **same optimization path (at least, concerning the empty projection one) as the first query**:

```
Rule analysis.Analyzer$ResolveRefs applied
Keep[[?salary]]                           ! EsqlProject[[salary{r}#67]]
\_Eval[[1[INTEGER] AS salary]]            = \_Eval[[1[INTEGER] AS salary]]
  \_Drop[[?salary]]     ----------------> !   \_EsqlProject[[]]
    \_EsRelation[employees][salary{f}#69] =     \_EsRelation[employees][salary{f}#69]
```

These two queries have something in common: **`ResolveRefs` evaluates the flavors of projections manipulation (keep, drop) as `EsqlProject[]` meaning no attributes as the output of a logicalPlan node in the tree**.

`PruneEmptyPlans` optimization rule then kicks in makes both queries as local relations.
For the first query the result (correct) is

```
       c       
---------------
0
```

For the second query the result (wrong) is

```
    salary     
---------------
```

When [we improved the performance of the _field_caps calls in ES|QL](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/98987) and we switched from asking all the fields' mapping to asking it only for the necessary fields, we also **lost the ability to tell if the user removed all the ES fields from a query or not** and the two queries above stand proof for this. The fact that we don't know for some queries how many fields an index or index pattern has, we cannot tell if `drop whatever` removes everything there is or not. For the very specific case of `keep X | drop X` (and some variants) we can tell, but for `from test | drop X | eval X = 1 | keep X` this can both drop all fields (let's say `test` only has one field - `X`) or drop just one (if `test` has `X` and `Y` fields in it).

---

#### What has all of this to do with the original report in this issue?

```
FROM languages
| DROP language_code
| EVAL language_code = 3
| LOOKUP JOIN languages_lookup ON language_code
| KEEP language_code
```

`PruneEmptyPlans` does the same thing to this query, because `drop language_code` results in an empty projection:

```
Rule analysis.Analyzer$ResolveRefs applied
Keep[[?language_code]]                                        ! EsqlProject[[language_code{r}#83]]
\_LookupJoin[LEFT OUTER USING [?language_code],[],[],[]]      ! \_LookupJoin[LEFT,[language_code{r}#83],[language_code{r}#83],[language_code{f}#87]]
  |_Eval[[3[INTEGER] AS language_code]]                       =   |_Eval[[3[INTEGER] AS language_code]]
  | \_Drop[[?language_code]]          ---------------->       !   | \_EsqlProject[[]]
  |   \_EsRelation[languages][language_code{f}#86]            =   |   \_EsRelation[languages][language_code{f}#86]
  \_EsRelation[languages_lookup][LOOKUP][language_code{f}#87] =   \_EsRelation[languages_lookup][LOOKUP][language_code{f}#87]
```

When [we improved the performance of the _field_caps calls in ES|QL](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/98987) imo we did it right. For the query above **we only need `language_code` from ES** to be able to determine the correctness of the query, we don't need all the fields.

Knowing how many fields `languages` actually has in its mapping could probably help us in differentiating the two use cases above.
